samples.marker_line: pyyi 2.5.4: correct payload, XOR and command-text traits
evidence: Wheel console_scripts declares python3.7 = pyyi.cli:main; METADATA advertises cryptographic primitives that __init__.py does not implement.

_baked_hosts decodes Base64 and repeating-key XOR into a JSON list of two space-z.ai hosts; PY3_SERVER or PY2_SERVER can override these. Both versions decode to the same hosts, with different packed bytes and keys.

_quiet_config silently bootstraps via _register, POSTing hostname and OS as op=1 to /api/update and saving the returned server/apiKey. api_json adds a host-derived MD5 tag. Candidate REPL words pass through _GateConsole.push -> _server_unlock -> api_json(op=2), as the password field. Terminal echo is suppressed through cbreak/_quiet_read, accepted words disappear, and rejected unknown words print 0.

Candidate filtering excludes keywords/helpers and multiline inputs but includes 1+1 and numeric tokens. Network-disabled mocks of the exact function definitions confirmed ReviewCanary987 and 1+1 are transmitted, while print("ordinary expression") is evaluated locally.

run_payload requests op=3, takes r["payload"], Base64-decodes, gzip-decompresses, compiles and execs the source in memory, then calls its main(argv). A synthetic response confirmed this execution path. Malformed payloads produced the fake python: can't open file error and exit status 2.

Uninstall is an explicit user-invoked removal path. The pip uninstall text is a displayed suggestion/comment, not proof that pip executes. Remote payloads were not fetched; their later actions remain unknown. The deceptive REPL export and failure concealment independently establish malicious behavior.

samples.marker_line: StormAttack loader: separate signature mismatch from hostile code
evidence: PE32 x86 MSVC/MFC StormAttack loader. The collector filename mentions Elex/WannaCry; the executable code and StormAttack banner/configuration identify this retained loader. No ransom/encryption claim is justified.

CRT entry 0x402674 reaches dispatcher 0x401cb0. DWORD 0x404120 is 3, selecting 0x401900 then self-delete routine 0x401390. Mode 3 generates a GUID destination, builds an Active Setup Installed Components subkey, writes StubPath as REG_EXPAND_SZ at 0x401a4b, reads its own image, patches/copies it with fread/fwrite, and calls CreateProcessA at 0x401b7e.

Alternate mode 1 attempts DLL resource 101 extraction through 0x402460 and file writer 0x4023c0. Routine 0x401260 deletes and replaces HKLM SYSTEM/CurrentControlSet/Services/LanmanServer/Parameters ServiceDLL with the StormServer.dll path. Routine 0x401150 creates an innocuous child, allocates remote memory, writes the DLL path, resolves Kernel32!LoadLibraryA and uses it as the remote thread entry at 0x40123d. Mode 2 contains automatic service creation/start via 0x401fd0.

0x401390 obtains its own module path, converts to an 8.3 short path, reads COMSPEC, assembles /c del with > nul, starts the command shell and resumes its thread. The retained injection, persistence and deletion implementation supports the hostile code traits without implying successful execution.

The entire .rsrc section is zero-filled (40960 raw bytes); IAT storage is partly overwritten by GUID text. This damaged specimen does not contain a recoverable working DDoS payload, and successful installation is not established.

The appended certificate names Microsoft and its signer cryptography verifies, but digest_matches is false. This does not show that Microsoft ever signed these image bytes, or distinguish transplant, corruption, and later modification. The generic fact is now suspicious signature metadata, with no hostile intent inferred. An inert control erasing all original .text/.data and retaining the certificate produces the mismatch findings and zero hostile traits.
The decoded percent-format GUID template is not an encoded network destination; the Microsoft HTTP URL is in the certificate. Neither establishes C2 traffic.
